For many animation artists and performers remembering Eric Bauza, the stories begin with his extraordinary voice and return to the same point: how he treated people.

Following Bauza’s death at 46, friends, collaborators, and fans have been sharing memories of his extraordinary talent and the kindness he brought to their lives.

We’ve collected some of those tributes below, bringing together recollections from across the animation community in one place. They describe a performer who treasured the characters entrusted to him, made time for the people around him, and shared his love of cartoons at every opportunity.

His fiancée, Caro Beurmann, founder of Saturday Morning Cartoons United, one of our favorite initiatives of the last several years, reflected on the organization they built together around animation and charitable causes. Its events have included a Care Bears Movie screening supporting animation workers affected by California’s wildfires and a Powerpuff Girls reunion fundraiser announced earlier this fall.

I know Eric would have wanted that mission to continue in some capacity, and I hope we can find a way to honor his legacy by continuing to support and uplift one another.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Saturday Morning Cartoons United™ (@cartoonsunited)

Coyote vs. Acme director Dave Green remembered a collaborator whose connection with audiences came from being a lifelong cartoon fan himself. Green accompanied his tribute with a video of Bauza performing karaoke at the film’s premiere afterparty.

He spent time with fans. Listened to them, hung out with them, enjoyed them. Because he was one of them.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Dave Green (@davegreeen)

In a joint statement, Warner Bros. Television Group chairman Channing Dungey and WBPA president and chief creative officer Bill Damaschke said:

Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world. During his 15 years at Warner Bros. Animation, he was the voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck among countless other characters. He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life. In addition to his incredible talent, Eric was a treasured part of our animation family. Our hearts go out to his loved ones.

In an emotional video, Phineas and Ferb co-creator and Dr. Doofenshmirtz voice actor Dan Povenmire recalled how hard it was to find performers who could fully embody Mel Blanc’s Looney Tunes characters when he was working with that property at Warner Bros. He felt Bauza had done that and spoke about seeing his talent gain wider recognition.

I just love the fact that somebody as nice, as just genuinely kind and nice as Eric was getting the success that he deserved.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Dan Povenmire (@dan.povenmire)

Jorge Gutiérrez, co-creator of El Tigre: The Adventures of Manny Rivera, remembered the excitement of developing characters for Bauza, who voiced Rodolfo Rivera/White Pantera in El Tigre.

I would write and design characters giddy thinking how he would bring them to life. And behind the scenes, an incredibly kind, humble and open-hearted good dude.

Voice actor Carlos Alazraqui, who worked with Bauza on The Fairly OddParents, shared memories of Bauza drawing pictures for his daughters and making friends laugh. To describe Bauza’s exceptional abilities, he made a musical comparison.

All the right notes, the perfect amount of notes. Not to be repeated, just a one-of-a-kind, wonderful human being.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Carlos Alazraqui (@carlosalazraqui)

Hundreds have posted their condolences and memories on the Instagram post on Bauza’s account that first announced his passing.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by 𝙀𝙍𝙄𝘾 𝘽𝘼𝙐𝙕𝘼 (@bauzilla)

Among them, Chris Prynoski, animation director and co-founder of Titmouse, expressed shock at losing someone he saw just a day earlier.

I just saw him yesterday. He was a great person, a great talent, and a great friend.

 Gravity Falls creator and voice actor Alex Hirsch shared a personal reminder of Bauza’s generosity and his ability to bring familiar characters into the lives of those around him.

The only thing bigger than Eric’s talent was his heart. He was so genuine and generous with his time and made every room he stepped in brighter. I still have voice memos he sent me on my phone as Bugs & Daffy.

Dana Terrace, creator of Disney’s The Owl House, remembered the warmth of their encounters.

He was always so kind and enthusiastic wherever I saw him. What an absolute tragedy, my heart goes out to his family.

Actor Vincent Martella, the voice of Phineas in Phineas and Ferb, described Bauza as a colleague whose company and experience he valued.

A tremendously talented and kind coworker who I always had great conversations with and learned from.

If you have a memory of Eric you’d like to share, or if you’ve seen any we missed, please leave it in the comments below. Whether you worked with him, met him at an event, or knew him through his performances, we’d love to hear as many stories as possible about one of animation’s greatest champions.

Travis Knight’s Wildwood opened with $12.2 million domestically over the October 23–25 weekend, according to distributor Fathom Entertainment. That total, while hardly blockbuster business, did outpace many of the industry’s more cautious estimates.

Laika’s PG-13 stop-motion feature ranked third behind Clayface ($24 million) and You Can See Everything ($19.5 million), averaging $4,162 per theater across the 2,942 locations reported by Fathom.

For context, among the studio’s previous domestic releases, Wildwood more than doubled Missing Link’s $5.9 million opening in 2019 and came close to Kubo and the Two Strings’ $12.6 million debut in 2016. In its box office report, Fathom also points to similar starts for Migration ($12.5 million) and the PG-13 The Bob’s Burgers Movie ($12.4 million), though comparable openings alone say little about eventual profitability. Some movies have better legs than others, and Laika’s films have often benefited from extended runs.

Worldwide, Rentrak’s estimates put Wildwood at $14.7 million, ranking fourth over the weekend. That figure includes an $11.8 million domestic estimate rather than Fathom’s revised total. Substituting the updated domestic figure would bring the worldwide tally to approximately $15.2 million, assuming the international estimate remains unchanged. Additional international markets will get the film over the coming weeks.

Audience response during exit polling offers reason for optimism. Fathom reports an A CinemaScore and five-star Rentrak exit polling, alongside a Sunday decline of just 13% from Saturday. Those are promising early indicators, but one weekend doesn’t establish a film’s staying power. Against a reported $100 million production budget, Wildwood has a long way to go toward theatrical profitability.

That said, Laika has more room than many producers to take the long view. Backed by the biollionaire Knight family, the studio has built an enduring audience for its films. Merchandise, licensing, events, and theatrical rereleases provide opportunities to keep earning well beyond an initial run, even if their contribution to individual films’ profitability isn’t publicly known.

The clearest example is Coraline, whose 2024 rerelease generated $52.4 million worldwide, 15 years after its original debut. That doesn’t guarantee a similar future for Wildwood, but it demonstrates why opening-weekend receipts tell only part of the story for Laika.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Alexandra Myotte and Jean-Sébastien Hamel’s What We Leave Behind (Ce qu’on laisse derrière), produced by Sémaphore Films in Canada. The filmmakers behind the standout A Crab in the Pool (2023) use hand-drawn 2D animation to explore sexual violence against men and the difficult process of confronting childhood trauma. The film qualified for Oscar consideration by winning Best International Short at the 2026 Kaboom Animation Festival.

Dan has a gaping hole in his neck that will not heal, a wound he can neither explain nor discuss. Returning to the sinister hockey arena of his childhood, he must confront the part of himself he left there. Trembling lines, disorienting perspectives, and colors that shift from darkness to radioactive brightness turn the rink into an expression of his inner life, making the lasting effects of abuse physically visible.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Alexandra Myotte: In Canada, hockey is almost a religion, and sexual scandals involving players and coaches have left a kind of hidden collective trauma. Like our previous film, A Crab in the Pool, What We Leave Behind explores how personal trauma shapes who we become and the paths toward healing; this time it’s about introspection. As one of too few animated shorts addressing sexual violence against men, we were driven by three intentions: that survivors feel heard and understood, that witnesses are moved to intervene, and that potential aggressors recognize the harm they cause and never act on it.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

Jean-Sébastien Hamel: We conducted extensive research into the healing process of assault survivors and realized how complex it can be. Wanting authenticity, I used the Deep Voice screenwriting technique, which allows me to dig deep within myself to reach repressed traumas, like having been bullied. This was channeled onto the screen and proved very constructive in terms of self-knowledge. The audience response was just as powerful: many viewers told us, through tears, how deeply the film resonated with them, that we had told their story and that it helps them move forward. We were really moved by all of them.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

Alexandra Myotte: What We Leave Behind is traditional 2D animation, drawn by hand, frame by frame. Given the visceral nature of the story, we chose a stripped-back, deliberately rough look: trembling lines, a heavy reliance on POV shots, and solid colors that shift between pitch-black darkness and radioactive glow, to vividly illustrate what is poisoning the protagonist’s life. The aesthetic is unpretentious by design to serve the film’s subject, bringing to the fore the way traumas are felt through time. Therefore, this deliberate rawness of the technique becomes an authentic mirror of a troubled inner life.

Hockey is such an important part of Canadian identity, but the rink becomes a place of trauma and silence in your film. How much did the sport’s culture and history of abuse influence the story?

Jean-Sébastien Hamel: We had a script for What We Leave Behind, and at first, the film wasn’t about hockey at all. But when Team Canada junior players were recently accused of a group sexual assault, our reaction was immediate. We had to do our part to help by telling this story that, unfortunately, so many people have lived through. Personally, as a kid, I played hockey and witnessed part of this reality without knowing what to do. So, making this film was our opportunity to do something more, hopefully contributing to making a better world.

The Animation Showcase has launched its 2026 collection, making 15 animated shorts available to stream for free for verified animation and film industry professionals.

The selection brings together festival titles ranging from six to 21 minutes, giving industry viewers a chance to catch films they missed on the circuit or revisit them during awards season. Access requires registration and verification of professional credentials.

Featured shorts include Anna Mantzaris’s Please, which recently won the shorts Special Jury Prize at Animation Is Film, and Stephen P. Neary’s Living with a Visionary, which won the animation short jury awards at both Sundance and AFI Fest.

The collection also includes Apart, directed by Pola Maneli and co-written by Spike Lee, and God Is Shy. Apart follows a friendship between two boys in apartheid South Africa, with a creative team that includes music supervisor Black Coffee and costume designer Laduma Ngxokolo.

Alongside the 15-film collection, the platform offers curated sections dedicated to Miyu and the National Film Board of Canada. Across all the platform’s selections, available titles include Acid City, Bread Will Walk, Corpus Christi, Cosmonauts, Dog Alone, The End, Once Upon a Body, Paradaïz, Praying Mantis, Saba, Sulaimani, What We Leave Behind, and more.

The collection arrives as The Animation Showcase marks its tenth anniversary. Founded by curator Benoit Berthe Siward, the organization combines curated screenings with promotion and awards strategy for animated shorts and features. Its industry streaming platform launched during the Covid-19 lockdown and now has more than 50,000 verified professionals, according to the organization.

“When I started The Animation Showcase 10 years ago, the ambition was simple: to help remarkable animated films reach the audiences they deserve,” Berthe Siward said in a statement. “That passion continues to guide every collection we curate.”

Previous films hosted on the platform include Flee, Marcel the Shell with Shoes On, Memoir of a Snail, Arco, and Little Amélie, alongside Oscar-winning shorts such as The Windshield Wiper and In the Shadow of the Cypress.

Existing members can sign in to watch the collection. New viewers can request free access through Cartoon Brew’s sign-up link. Applicants must provide an email address and evidence of industry work, such as an IMDb, LinkedIn, or Vimeo profile. Once approved, they will receive an email with instructions on how to access the platform.

WIA NYC Animation Festival Returns For Third Year, Celebrating Animation And Community

By Cartoon Brew Connect | 10/26/2026 2:23 pm | Be the First to Comment!

  • Share
  • Tweet
  • Email

On November 1, WIA NYC brings together the greater New York City animation community to showcase 28 films by emerging student artists and established independent creators.

As part of WIA’s global community, WIA NYC brings the organization’s mission of connection, advocacy, and empowerment to the greater New York City animation community. Through the WIA NYC Animation Festival, the chapter creates a platform for animators and storytellers, with a particular focus on supporting people of underrepresented gender identities while welcoming everyone committed to a more inclusive and equitable animation industry.

On November 1, 2026, the WIA NYC Animation Festival returns to SVA Theatre for its third annual celebration of independent animation, storytelling, and creative collaboration. This year’s lineup features 28 animated films by local artists, bringing together student and professional work for an evening of screenings, networking, and community building. The program includes award-winning films such as Worcestershire Sauce by Dylan Baddeley, Coworker Crush by Ash Suh, Spiral by Abbey Lynn Paccia, and Our Pockets Are Full by Anjali Pulim.

This year’s festival centers on the theme of “Community,” highlighting WIA NYC’s commitment to building meaningful connections among local animators, filmmakers, students, and industry professionals. In addition to awards for best animation and best student animation, the festival will present an award for best community-themed animated film, recognizing films that explore the relationships, shared experiences, and collective interests that bring people together. ASIFA-East will also present its own “Best Of” award, continuing the organizations’ collaboration and shared commitment to supporting local filmmakers and recognizing outstanding animation.

Ashley Gerst, who founded the WIA NYC Animation Festival in 2024 while serving as co-lead of the WIA NYC chapter, shared her enthusiasm for the festival’s growth: “This is something that I’ve wanted to do for a long time. It’s truly exciting to see how much momentum the festival has gathered in the last two years. There is so much talent in the greater New York City area, and WIA NYC is honored to bring a small portion of it to the big screen where it can be celebrated and supported!”

Monica Joy, an animator and filmmaker whose work was selected for the inaugural festival in 2024, returned this year as a festival judge. Reflecting on the experience, Joy said, “It was a pleasure to be a judge for this year’s incredible festival lineup. Frankly, I was startled at the level of talent, inclusion, and thoughtfulness of both the filmmakers and event organizers. Nickelodeon’s The Loud House will continue into a tenth season, but its Los Angeles production crew won’t, according to longtime series director Jessica Borutski.

Speaking with Grim & Evil creator Maxwell Atoms on his YouTube series Billy & Mandy vs. The Entertainment Industry, Borutski said the show’s next production season would keep its showrunners but move production to Canada. She described the decision as a cost-cutting move.

“They didn’t hire any of the LA crew,” she said. “They’re sending all of the production work to Canada… They wanna make it, but cheaper.”

The move reflects a broader concern running through long parts of the conversation: animation work leaving Los Angeles, and artists questioning whether they can still build careers there, or at all. Borutski describes widespread unemployment among her colleagues and people leaving, while Atoms questions studios’ willingness to fund productions adequately.

While both speakers share concern about artificial intelligence, neither has seen direct examples of AI replacing workers in their studios, or even being implemented into workflows. “I don’t know any shows that are being made with assisted AI right now. There’s nothing. At least not at the typical Nickelodeons,” she says, before Disney Jr.’s Ozzy Fox, a collaboration with AI-focused company Animaj, as the lone exception that she’s aware of.

For artists, the uncertainty encompasses both where the work is going and whether a sustainable career will remain. “I wonder what the second half of my life’s going to look like,” Borutski says with a nervous laugh. “Will there still even be a Hollywood scene?”

“Does this just end up being something I do between shifts at the grocery store?” Atoms half-jokes in reply.

While both can laugh now, there’s real concern in their delivery, and in the delivery of just about every artist we’ve talked to over the past several years.

Four episodes into its 38th season, The Simpsons makes its annual pit stop for Halloween with “Treehouse of Horror XXXVII,” which aired October 25 on Fox and is streaming on Hulu.

Co-showrunner Tim Long took the lead in producing this year’s special, which opens with a bespoke stop-motion homage to The Nightmare Before Christmas before proceeding with three traditionally animated stories: “Bride’s Shed Revisited,” “Dog Boy Afternoon,” and “Vehicular Dad Slaughter.”

Cartoon Brew spoke with Long and the opening’s director, John Harvatine of Burbank, California-based Stoopid Buddy Stoodios, about bringing the episode to life with veteran director David Silverman (The Simpsons Movie).

With almost 30 years at The Simpsons, this year’s “Treehouse” is not Long’s first time up to the Halloween plate. However, there’s a quality bar that Long said rattles all of the producers. “It’s a little daunting because there is this incredible tradition that we have to uphold, and it’s always a very prominent episode in our schedule,” Long explained. “Apparently, it gets way more viewers than almost any other episode, so you’ve got to bring the goods. Plus, there’s also this tradition now that we want to do something different animation-wise.”

For the episode’s opening, Long said he was thinking about classic Disney Halloween films and realized they had never done a stop-motion riff on Henry Selick’s The Nightmare Before Christmas. “It has become such a perennial classic, and I love the animation style,” he explained. “We figured the [characters] are going to look great in that style. Plus, we had a preexisting relationship with Stoopid Buddy, so it felt like a no-brainer.”

Joining him to write “Treehouse of Horror XXXVII” were staff writers Joel H. Cohen and Jessica Conrad. Long said of their stories, “I’m always a little wary of just doing a parody of the latest horror movie. And the ground is pretty well stripped of the classics of horror. So, like a lot of things on The Simpsons, the ideas came up organically.”

Long said his segment, “Vehicular Dad Slaughter,” was inspired by classic driver’s education films featuring violent car-crash footage meant to terrify high school kids and new drivers. “I thought it was a funny idea, and it sort of led naturally to the idea of Patty and Selma — who work at the DMV — being the villains,” he explained. “We realized that after all these years, Patty and Selma had never been the villains in a ‘Treehouse of Horror,’ which struck me as a really funny omission.”

Conrad’s “Dog Boy Afternoon” came out of a Matt Groening mandate to “get back to the days when the Halloween episodes are genuinely scary.” Long said Conrad created a gnarly Pet Sematary-style story involving Santa’s Little Helper. “I made sure that when Homer swings the shovel and hits Bart in the head, that you really are like, ‘Wow, look at that. You don’t see that every day.’ Or when the dogs disembowel Homer, we wanted it to be super fast but really funny.”

Cohen’s “Bride’s Shed Revisited” is a twist on Holly Gramazio’s novel The Husbands, in which Marge discovers that the family’s new shed is a portal to different realities where she’s married to everyone except Homer. One of those husbands is Survivor host Jeff Probst, who Long said was enthusiastic about joining the fun. “We didn’t want to just go with a super hunk du jour,” he explained. “But someone who Marge would be really into.”

The Simpsons Before Christmas

The opening sequence combines two kinds of animation: stop-motion puppetry paired with Simpsons parody lyrics for “This Is Halloween,” and claymation titles.

Harvatine told Cartoon Brew that Matt Selman first floated the idea for a Nightmare homage in 2024, after Stoopid Buddy completed its stop-motion work on the “Treehouse of Horror” segment “Denim.”

“It was such early stages that he wasn’t sure if it was gonna happen,” Harvatine recalled. “So, we didn’t really talk about it in classic The Simpsons fashion until three months ago. They were like, ‘We want to talk about the opening for this.’ They talked about Nightmare, and I was like, ‘Oh, that’s amazing!’”

Silverman worked on-site with Harvatine and his team. “We sat with him, and I thought it would take a while to figure out how to get all these characters right,” Harvatine said. “But pretty quickly, he had his little sketch pad and would throw ideas out and did it pretty fast.”

The team immediately began fabricating 16 individual puppets, including doubles. “The real challenge was, how do we make puppets that we can do in a short amount of time, but make them feel worthy of Nightmare?” Harvatine said. “It was a real challenge for the puppet department. But the team really excelled and rose to the challenge. Right off the bat, they just started turning out these really beautiful sculpts and beautiful puppets. And then all of the costumes were hand-sewn. There were probably five or six different artists, and multiple sculpts going at the same time to make this happen. We had to have multiples of each puppet, so it was the longest process of everything, but once they started moving, it started working out all right.”

Long and his writers provided the song parody and a rough animatic of the sequence, which the Stoopid Buddy team used to develop the set and lighting. Stoopid Buddy also created a claymation title screen featuring letters made of worms, which Harvatine said almost didn’t happen. “We were hoping we could do it in clay, but that was a lot to do,” he explained. “Our backup was gonna be making a mold and spit them out the old-fashioned way. But we were doing pretty good on time, so we were able to hand-sculpt all those [worms].

“We saved time at the end, and we kept an animator on so we could have that really elaborate splat ending,” he continued. “What’s really fun too, if you freeze-frame on when they’re flying out, there are Simpsons Easter eggs in there. The animator had a lot of fun with it. And it’s always rewarding to find a way to put [claymation] into a project. I love the imperfection and the fingerprints and just the rawness of it.”

From the hand-stitched costumes to the quality of the animated performances, Harvatine said he’s proud that his team rose to the occasion to honor Selick and Tim Burton’s film. “We talked to the animators and were like, ‘Go big, go bold. Don’t worry about the little little feet, just really bring the performance,’” he said of several puppets that didn’t have tie-downs. “And I’m really proud of the animation team for how much they pushed things with what they had.”

Eric Bauza, the remarkably versatile voice actor who brought new life to some of animation’s most enduring characters and became one of the medium’s most passionate public advocates, died Sunday, October 25. He was 46. According to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records cited by Variety, the cause was hypertensive cardiovascular disease.

Bauza was among the busiest and most consequential voice actors of his era. His work reached across studios, franchises, and audiences, from preschool television to adult comedy, superhero adventures, and theatrical features. He had already built a career of extraordinary range, with every reason to expect decades of memorable performances still ahead.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by 𝙀𝙍𝙄𝘾 𝘽𝘼𝙐𝙕𝘼 (@bauzilla)

His importance went far beyond the number of characters he could perform. Bauza understood cartoons from sketch to screen. He knew their history, credited the people who made them, and used his growing visibility to advocate for their future. That enthusiasm was evident in his interviews, convention appearances, and animation programming

He was a performer who could make familiar characters feel immediately recognizable while also fitting them into contemporary situations and storylines. That combination made him an especially important steward of the Looney Tunes.

Born December 7, 1979, in Scarborough, Ontario, Bauza grew up in a Filipino immigrant family and watched Saturday morning cartoons with his brother. His interest in voices developed alongside his interest in drawing. Speaking with Caroline Cao for JoySauce, he recalled studying miniature reproductions of animation artwork in Chuck Jones gallery catalogs, using a magnifying glass to examine the characters. He also remembered recording messages that his family mailed to relatives in the Philippines, an early opportunity to play with a microphone.

That childhood fascination led him into animation production as he got older and began to think about a professional life. As he explained in a 2009 interview with Jason Anders for Fülle Circle, Bauza joined Spumco as a college intern in 1999–2000 while studying radio, television, and film at Centennial College. He worked as a production assistant and made his ambitions to perform voices abundantly clear.

An early opportunity arrived on The Ripping Friends. One of his first characters, Future Cat, also offered an unexpected Cartoon Brew connection: Bauza said in the Fülle Circle interview that he based the voice on this site’s co-founder, Amid Amidi.

In the interview, he explained:

For the voice, John thought it would be funny to base it off of a former Spumco colleague, and one of Cartoon Brew’s co-founders, Amid Amidi. Amid has a very distinct voice. I can’t explain what it sounds like without Amid killing me. You just have to hear him talk in person – it’s like magic. I thought it was a weird choice, but for some odd reason the voice worked.

Bauza subsequently played Stimpy in Ren & Stimpy “Adult Party Cartoon”, while contributing layouts and editing animatics. There, his cross-disciplinary work extended to music and sound effects, and he learned the rhythm of a sequence, how the separate elements of a cartoon performance fit together.

That experience matters in understanding his later career. In animation, a voice actor’s performance becomes part of a larger whole. Each pose, held expression, and sudden movement needs to work with the voice actor’s performance. Because Bauza had worked directly with those elements as a visual artist, he could approach a recording session with an appreciation of the artists who would turn his delivery into a finished scene.

His major early roles included Rodolfo Rivera, the heroic White Pantera and Manny’s father in Jorge R. Gutierrez and Sandra Equihua’s Emmy-winning El Tigre: The Adventures of Manny Rivera.

He later played Foop in The Fairly OddParents, Lord Stingray in Superjail!, Buhdeuce in Breadwinners, and Belly Bag in Uncle Grandpa. His action credits included Destro, Storm Shadow, and Tunnel Rat in G.I. Joe: Resolute, and Tiger Claw in Nickelodeon’s Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.

Bauza also inherited characters whose personalities audiences already knew intimately: the title character of The Adventures of Puss in Boots, Baby Fozzie in the reimagined Muppet Babies, and Woody Woodpecker in Universal’s feature films. His commercial work also included Saturday morning cereal mascots Lucky the Leprechaun and the Trix Rabbit.

Yet he was candid about the difference between impersonating a voice and acting a role. Speaking with Victoria Davis for Animation World Network in 2023, he said: “What gets you through that door and allows you to stay in the room is the good acting.”

He credited working alongside experienced performers and directors with helping him develop that ability. He described learning the craft through criticism, uncertainty, and the trust of collaborators who kept giving him opportunities.

His recurring relationship with Uncle Grandpa creator Pete Browngardt proved especially significant. In a 2015 Comic-Con roundtable, Bauza recalled first encountering Browngardt’s original short while working at his drawing desk. The cartoon interrupted his work because it immediately made him want to collaborate with its creator. Years later, that relationship would extend into Browngardt’s Looney Tunes Cartoons and The Day the Earth Blew Up.

Bauza had begun voicing Marvin the Martian on The Looney Tunes Show in 2011. His responsibilities eventually expanded to Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweety, Porky Pig, and numerous others across different productions. In Space Jam: A New Legacy, he voiced Daffy, Porky, Foghorn Leghorn, Elmer Fudd, and Marvin.

Filling the shoes of legends like Mel Blanc required careful judgment. These characters carry decades of accumulated expectations, but their performances must still serve the scene and the larger story. Bugs needs confidence and comic timing; Daffy needs the conviction that his latest unreasonable demand is entirely justified. A recognizable voice might catch a viewer’s attention, but the actor’s performance is what will keep them watching.

Bauza’s work on The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie offered an impressive and concentrated demonstration of that skill. Playing both Daffy and Porky, he brought the two sides of a relationship to life. In the same scene, he would deftly deliver the instigator and the worrier, the explosive reaction and the hesitant reply, the aggravation and the affection.

Speaking with Rachael Harper for SciFiNow, Bauza said he recorded Porky first to preserve his voice before tackling Daffy’s more demanding outbursts. He also emphasized the years of collaboration behind the film, crediting Browngardt, Alex Kirwan, and the artists and writers whose work gave him the foundation for those performances.

His contributions received increasing recognition. Bauza won three Children’s & Family Emmy Awards for Looney Tunes Cartoons, Bugs Bunny Builders, and his performances as Bugs and Daffy in Teen Titans Go!

According to the Variety obituary, at the time of his death, Bauza was in pre-production on Bye Bye Bunny: A Looney Tunes Musical and The Dragon Masters. In August 2024, Bauza posted a recording of the singing audition he said landed him the role in the former.

Here’s my singing audition that helped me book “Bye Bye Bunny: A Looney Tunes Musical ” — with screenplay and lyrics by Emmy Award winner Ariel Dumas (The Late Show with Stephen Colbert) and music and orchestration by Pulitzer Prize, Tony and Grammy winner Tom Kitt (Next to Normal). Wish we could’ve seen this one come to fruition — would’ve been a good one 🎞️ 🎥 🍿 🥕🐰#StandWithAnimation @papertiki

— Eric Bauza (@bauzilla) August 17, 2024

Bauza’s public-facing career carried particular significance for Filipino and Asian audiences, and he knew it. Bauza became the first person of color to voice Bugs Bunny, prompting an enthusiastic response from viewers who recognized themselves in the person behind the microphone.

He understood why that mattered. In the JoySauce interview, he welcomed the possibility that his career could encourage people who felt unheard or assumed such opportunities were unavailable to them:

I like that there was a reaction, and there were people that were very proud and excited to see a person of color in the driver’s seat. And for me, no matter what your heritage is, no matter what you look like, no matter what your cultural background is, if this is a story that allows you to use your voice or encourages you to use your voice—if you’re shy to use your voice, or you feel like you’re not heard—then I feel like it’s a story that will inspire you in that way. It’s a positive thing and a good thing that encourages people, who didn’t think they have a chance, that it is possible.

As a performer passionate about the history of his craft, Bauza’s love of animation also included a willingness to examine its shortcomings. In hosting the CBC documentary series Stay Tooned, Bauza explored representation, stereotypes, sexuality, and commercialism in cartoons, speaking with artists and commentators about the ideas embedded in entertainment that audiences often first encounter as children.

Speaking with Pat Mullen for POV, he explained: “It’s good to talk about them, examine them, and learn from them as opposed to sweeping them under the rug.”

He also discussed the need for authentic representation behind the microphone and in storytelling, and challenged the tendency to dismiss animation’s importance to adult audiences.

When Warner Bros. shelved Coyote vs. Acme, Bauza became a public advocate for its release. At the 2024 Annie Awards, he brought that campaign to the stage in Daffy Duck’s voice.

In interviews, he repeatedly returned to the care these characters deserved. In a September interview with Movieland, he said, “Every time I hop into the booth to do something new with these characters, it’s like being on the job for the first day.”

Bauza is survived by his son. Fatherhood had added another dimension to his work, he said in the AWN interview, including a growing affection for preschool programming and the experience of watching cartoons together. His son, he said, could recognize his voice even in shows Bauza had forgotten recording.

Bauza’s death is an enormous loss for animation, both in the recording booth and in the public conversation around the medium. He helped keep historic characters alive through new performances, supported the artists creating their next adventures, and shared the pleasure of that work with audiences. Although cut far shorter than it should have been, he leaves behind a remarkable legacy that overshadows any individual role he played.

China’s first fully AI-generated theatrical feature, its producers claim, has flopped at the box office, perhaps reminding financiers that enthusiasm for the technology doesn’t necessarily translate into demand from moviegoers.

Estimates show that Bona Film Group’s Sanxingdui: Future Past earned just RMB1.21 million ($181,000) through Monday, after its October 23 debut. According to Bona, the science-fiction feature cost more than RMB10 million ($1.5 million) and required nearly 100 people working for over two years. More than 10,000 screenings were scheduled for opening day, giving it ample opportunity to find an audience.

Notably, the dismal launch comes two months after Chinese audiences embraced a very different animation curiosity in Niu Lai, a shoestring feature made by director Xin Yumeng and his mother, screenwriter Sun Lifang.

That film barely made a peep when it first hit theaters, earning roughly RMB7,700 ($1,150) during its first ten days after opening on August 5. But then clips of its crude modeling, stiff animation, and bizarre performances spread online. Its shortcomings became its charm, transforming an obscure production into a communal moviegoing experience with an oddly endearing pair of filmmakers behind it.

Niu Lai has now grossed RMB64.29 million, or nearly $10 million. A direct comparison of grosses is perhaps premature, given its own slow start, but its August breakout demonstrated that Chinese audiences would buy tickets to an animated film with almost none of the visual sophistication producers and distributors typically consider essential.

To be clear, we’re not claiming either film’s performance establishes a universal rule about audiences’ attitudes toward AI. Niu Lai benefited from initial mockery, memes, and curiosity as much as affection. Still, its eccentric humanness gave moviegoers something they wanted to experience together. Sanxingdui’s claim to represent a filmmaking breakthrough has proved considerably less compelling to audiences looking for movie magic.

In 1983, animation producer John Coates issued a one-page pitch for a new project developed with executive producer Iain Harvey. The document was typed beneath the sweet, fuzzy letterhead of “Snowman Enterprises,” the then-current name for TV Cartoons’ production wing, which had recently produced the Oscar-nominated animated short based on Raymond Briggs’ illustrated children’s book, The Snowman. The plan, this time, was for a much darker, feature-length adaptation of a 1982 Briggs creation.

When the Wind Blows was a deadpan, adult-themed comic strip about a homey elderly couple, Jim and Hilda Bloggs, experiencing a nuclear attack. As outlined in the pitch, the 85-minute film dealt with “the most potent human issue facing us—the human consequences of a nuclear attack.” The pitch went on to describe the tenor of Briggs’ vision: “In a devastating and comic manner, but totally without rancor or political viewpoint, it attacks the hypocritical manner in which the consequences of a nuclear war are minimized by nearly all governments.”

To direct the film, Coates enlisted his longtime collaborator Jimmy T. Murakami. The stout and silver-haired Japanese American, Oscar-nominated for his 1967 animated short Breath, had been supervising director of The Snowman (with Dianne Jackson), director of TVC’s “Soft Landing” opening for the animated sci-fi film Heavy Metal (1981), and director of Roger Corman’s live-action Star Wars/Seven Samurai mashup, Battle Beyond the Stars (1980).

Murakami was drawn to the dark wit and trenchant themes of Briggs’ book. Working from Briggs’ screenplay, Murakami roughed out storyboards, and TVC produced a three-minute test. Murakami proposed a bold visual treatment. Inspired by Fleischer Studios’ “Stereoptical” or “setback” process—developed nearly four decades earlier for Betty Boop, Popeye, and Superman cartoons—the film physically layered hand-drawn 2D cel animation over stop-motion-animated 3D model backgrounds.

When the Wind Blows went on to win the Grand Prix at Annecy in 1987. Briggs, Coates, and Murakami are no longer with us, but their work went on to achieve cult status and still lives today in TikTok memes. To mark the 40th anniversary of the film’s U.K. release on October 24, Cartoon Brew persuaded one of its staff writers (who toiled in the When the Wind Blows cutting room) to hunt down other survivors of TVC’s animation crew. Read on, in this special two-part story, to learn from animation art director Richard Fawdry and then-animation assistant Paul Donnellon (now co-founder of Voodoodog) what went down at Meltdown Productions.

Part One: Backgrounds

Cartoon Brew (Joe Fordham): Richard, you wore many hats at Meltdown, including animation designer, layout designer, storyboard artist, and art director with Errol Bryant. How did you get started at TVC?

Richard Fawdry: I joined TVC in 1979. It was my first job out of college. I did a little animation on Heavy Metal, and I was working on a show called Castles (1983) when they made The Snowman. That was exciting to watch because it was evident Snowman was going to be really good. Toward the end of that, I did some uncredited rendering—I’m not going to say which bits because my work was horrendous [laughs]. They were so desperate at the end to get it done, they let anyone work on it.

Was that your doorway into When the Wind Blows?

Fawdry: That’s right. I did cleanup on Jimmy’s storyboards. I then went away for a year to get married. I was on an island when I got a phone call to come back. That’s when they announced how they were going to shoot the backgrounds. Before I went away, I’d done a plan of Jim and Hilda’s house to help with traditional painted layouts. When I returned, I discovered that someone must have found that handy as a starting point for the model backgrounds.

What was it like working with Jimmy Murakami?

Fawdry: Out of all the directors I’ve worked with, he was the most enterprising with all the different techniques that he came up with for the film. He was very easygoing, but he knew what he wanted. He was in control all the time. And he was quite firm.

Paul, you met Jimmy when you were at school in Ireland. How did that happen?

Paul Donnellon: Jimmy had a studio in Dublin doing commercials. I was at the Institute of Art, Design and Technology, the only one doing animation on their graphic design course when Jimmy visited as a lecturer. I became his stalker. For a year, I worked for free at his studio, helping out in my spare time, and I used to go on shoots. When I graduated from IADT, Jimmy took me to London. It was my first job. I’d never been to London before. It was mad, in crowded Soho.

How did the idea of shooting miniature backgrounds come about?

Fawdry: Well, Jimmy did that lot. On Heavy Metal, he directed the opening sequence with a car falling down from space, where he shot a live-action car. As a live-action director, he liked to set up a camera. So, even though the house was in miniature, he set up all the scenes how he wanted.

Donnellon: He also told me he loved the Fleischer Superman cartoons from the 1930s that had real model sets. That influenced him, I think.

The “A.R.S.” photo-background process has been well documented—with Peter Turner and lighting director Ken Friswell on the model shoot, making 17,000 glossy, 12-by-10-inch 3M prints pin-registered for Peter’s rostrum camera at TVC. What do you remember about that—and was “A.R.S.” really an acronym, or Pete’s rude joke?

Donnellon: [Laughs] I don’t know. Martin Howard was the photo man who used to come into TVC. He organized all the printing.

Fawdry: There was a cost consideration to that. I remember it was going to be £100 or £500 per [painted] background, and when they added it up, doing the photo prints was £75,000. So, it was half the price to print photo backgrounds.

Donnellon: They printed black-and-white Xeroxes of the photographs so the animators wouldn’t ruin them. We ended up getting Xeroxes punched and registered for each background. The line tests all had Xerox backgrounds of photo plates, which gave them a “Xeroxey” look with the line test on top.

Fawdry: Yes, that was important for moving shots.

Did either of you attend the miniature shoot?

Fawdry: I visited once. All I remember is they had some really nice food.

Donnellon: Oh, yeah, they had a buffet, and [production coordinator] Anne Goodall was there. Jimmy took me because I was his assistant. We spent ages there [10 weeks]. It was interesting because they had the model on a big turntable. To get a moving shot, they rotated the set frame by frame. It wasn’t motion control. It was an ancient [hybrid Bell/Mitchell] camera from 1916.

Who built the miniatures?

Fawdry: That was Errol Bryant. I went to his house while he was building those. His whole house was full of models that he was making. My friend Joan Ashworth made little stuffed dolls of Jim and Hilda [used for blocking].

They also had models for interstitial scenes of a B-52 bomber, an ICBM rocket, and a nuclear submarine—did Errol make those, too?

Fawdry: Yes, he made all those. I remember when they brought back that film—it was either the bomber or the submarine—it came up to camera, it looked really good—and then it went bonk on the camera lens. They were really well made.

I was impressed by how the house had a painterly finish like Raymond Briggs’ drawings. Was that Errol’s doing?

Fawdry: Yes. That was a huge amount of work. I believe Errol had some help, maybe from his wife, and he sent away for details like cutlery. He was also a background artist [on this film, Heavy Metal, and Watership Down (1978)].

Part Two: Animation

To appreciate how this 40-year-old movie was made, we should note that every frame of Jim and Hilda was hand-drawn and painted—correct?

Donnellon: Yes. It was all inked by hand, wasn’t it, Richard?

Fawdry: Yes, we had lots of inkers at TVC. And the characters were animated on twos.

Were the model backgrounds also shot on twos?

Donnellon: Yeah, they shot the model on twos, but then they printed every second photograph to save money on the prints. Except panning shots and camera moves [characters and backgrounds] were animated on ones, weren’t they, Richard?

Fawdry: They had to be; otherwise, they’d strobe.

TVC had a superstar lineup of animators. Back then, I was surprised by how many Canadians there were. They were a great bunch, but how come?

Donnellon: Sheridan [College in Ontario] was the best animation school at the time. I now think Gobelins [School of Imagery] has the lead in Paris; they have trained so many really good animators. Jimmy was always moaning about U.K. animators. He liked Canadian animation because it wasn’t clichéd, or he thought they had more acting ability—I don’t think that was necessarily true, but Jimmy thought that way.

Do you recall who animated which sequences?

Fawdry: Yes, I made a list. Malcolm Draper did the early scenes in the bus, and with Jim at home with Hilda [saying “Crumbs!”] at the threat-of-war announcement. Dave Unwin did Jim painting the windows, which I thought was lovely. Tony Guy did a lot of wonderful work with Hilda ironing and saying, “It’s going to be drafty with no doors.” He was animation director on Watership Down, a really good animator.

Donnellon: Who was the man who developed his line tests in a bucket? And he lived in Stroud?

Fawdry: Dave Unwin and Tony Guy lived there. But I believe you’re thinking of Harold Whitaker. He did scenes just after the bomb. Harold was probably one of the best animators ever. He worked on Animal Farm (1954), and he wrote a textbook on animation [Timing for Animation, co-authored with John Halas in 1981]. His timing and acting were the best.

Bill Speers was another Canadian. He lived on a barge at Canary Wharf. He did the scary scenes just prior to and including the three-minute warning—from Jim saying, “Who’s in charge now?” to Hilda saying, “The cake will be burned.”

John McGuire was Australian and did scenes of Jim and Hilda in the shelter. He had the derring-do attitude of an adventurer, a buccaneering spirit. He got me the job at TVC, actually. And then, when I was still at college, he asked me to design some characters, and he left the country before he paid me! [Laughs] But he came back and paid me what he owed me. There was a rumor he was sick. I remember his assistant, who was also a Canadian, told me John was worried about his health. As it turned out, sadly, John died of cancer.

Was it John McGuire who made that fantastic dessert for the TVC Christmas party? That trifle had more rum in it than trifle!

Fawdry: Yes, that was a proper trifle.

Donnellon: I remember Roger Mainwood. He went on to direct Ethel & Ernest [the 2016 animated feature from Raymond Briggs’ memoir].

Fawdry: That’s right. Roger animated the very first scenes with Jim reading the newspaper in the library and coming back from shopping to buy a set square to measure the angle of the “inner core or refuge” [bomb shelter]. Hilary Audus did scenes where Jim walks up the pathway to the house and inside their hallway. Jo Harrison—née Fryer—did exteriors with Jim and Hilda walking in their garden before and after the bomb [and Jim as a truck driver in the Blitz, with other scenes by Michael Salkeld and Vanessa Clegg]. And Stephen Weston was a fantastic animator. He did the bomb blast.

Steve also did the flying sequence on Snowman, but the bomb sequence was something else. It was extraordinary how Steve animated geometric objects. Do you know how he did that?

Fawdry: He used models so he could turn them around [for perspectives]. I remember the models were plastic because he used one as an ashtray. Steve worked at the top of TVC, up in the attic, and at some point he stubbed a cigarette out in his model and it started a fire [laughs]. He used to blow things up. He filmed lots of explosions as reference for the bomb. Or maybe that was an excuse! He did that with [TVC in-house film editor] Taylor Grant. They enjoyed themselves.

It surprised me when they rendered that bomb sequence with a raw, scratchy quality—what inspired that choice?

Fawdry: It was something to do with [documentary] footage they had of a nuclear explosion. They took that as reference for the effects of the blast on houses, trees, and other things. At least, that’s how it looked to me. And then they rendered it to show the tremendous heat in the blast.

Donnellon: Yeah, they shaded that on paper, Xeroxed it onto cels, and then they rubbed bits off the cels to distress it. I remember Steve doing something with a Brillo pad [dishwashing scourer] to scratch up the surfaces.

Fawdry: That’s right. But no sheep were hurt in this film.

When the blast hits, you had a fantastic sequence, Richard, that I always thought was so quintessentially you—where Jim and Hilda’s old wedding photos come alive in a sweet and nostalgic way. How did you translate that from Raymond Briggs’ drawings?

Fawdry: That sequence wasn’t in Raymond Briggs’ book. It was another of Jimmy’s inspired ideas. He briefed me verbally with a quick outline, no drawings, and I went ahead and drew Jim and Hilda’s past, trying to keep to Raymond Briggs’ style. Loraine Marshall [and Milly McMillan] then rendered that to look like old photos.

Donnellon: You also animated Monty [World War II Field Marshal Bernard Law Montgomery]. Was he in that sequence?

Fawdry: Oh, I animated Monty for another scene. I did that after I finished all the animation layouts. And, of course, you worked on the Russian with Joe Ekers.

Donnellon: Yes, bursting through the door. I did all the inbetweens on that.

Paul, I know you were close with people in the layout team, weren’t you?

Donnellon: Oh, yeah. Giorgio Mardegan, John Watkiss, Dassos Petrou. Das had a blazing row with Jimmy about three-point perspective. They argued for ages about some technical Renaissance idea of perspective—both were correct, but using different terms. John Watkiss did storyboards and layouts. He was too good an artist to draw Jim and Hilda as pinheads, so in his drawings he gave them proper skull shapes. John did concept work for Disney’s Tarzan (1999). He was also a very famous comic book artist [The Sandman (1992)]. He was 55 when he died.

Dianne Jackson—who also sadly died too young—had another highlight of the film: Hilda’s dream, which showed Hilda’s inner life of naughty little cherubs. Do you remember how she animated that, and were you part of that, Richard?

Fawdry: No, that was all Dianne’s. Jimmy was quite surprised when he got that back. He asked her about it, and she said, “Oh, you wouldn’t understand, you’re not a woman.” It was very personal to her. She did that by drawing straight onto paper, I think in crayon. I’m wondering now if Jill Brooks, the wife of Stuart Brooks, might have helped. But I didn’t storyboard any of that. Dianne did that on her own.

That was especially lovely with Roger Waters’ music. Roger was one of many famous people who visited TVC. Do you remember that celebrity parade?

Fawdry: Yes, [actors] Sir John Mills and Dame Peggy Ashcroft came to visit, and we showed them storyboards. Jeremy Isaacs, the chief of Channel 4, stopped by. And Paul and Linda McCartney. I remember Paul stroking Joe Ekers’ long, frizzy hair. He’d worked with Joe before on Rupert and the Frog Song [a music video directed by Geoff Dunbar in 1984].

Was it Joe who did some funny sketches of Jim and Hilda?

Donnellon: I think so. There was a wall where people would stick drawings. There was one of them in the bathtub together.

Moving quickly past that, I have to ask: What do you think has kept this film in public consciousness after 40 years?

Donnellon: I think Russia going to war with Ukraine has brought it back, and the threat of nuclear war. Do you remember, Richard, when the Chernobyl disaster happened [April 26, 1986]? We were scared because it was all about radiation coming in and acid rain in Wales.

Fawdry: Yes. I do remember when détente happened [Gorbachev mellowing Soviet relations with Europe], I was thankful and relieved, like the rest of the world, but that was just before When the Wind Blows’ release, and I think Russia’s reduced hostility affected the impact of the film. There were protests against the film because some people thought we were “anti-bomb.” Well, the story is about using a bomb, and that was what it’s meant to be: a deterrent. I couldn’t understand the uproar.

How do you two look back on the film, and have you shown it to your kids?

Donnellon: Richard and I went to a screening last year. In June 2025, there was a “Bleak Week” festival of depressing films here in London. It was really good to see it fresh. I’ve not shown it to my sons yet. My wife says if our boys are annoying, I’ll make them watch it one day [laughs].

Fawdry: My children haven’t seen it either, and they are 37! I do look back on the film with pride. It was great making friends, and the camaraderie was good. We’ve stayed friends since then. It’s still one of the few adult animated films made here in the U.K.

When the Wind Blows is available on DVD and Blu-ray from the British Film Institute.

Meltdown Editorial – A Sidebar With TVC Editor Taylor Grant

As When the Wind Blows took shape in TV Cartoons’ editorial basement, producer John Coates’ longtime in-house film editor, Taylor Grant, ran the studio’s main cutting room upstairs. If I was the meek dormouse down below, Taylor was John’s Mad Hatter—a tall, creative fellow with a rich Canadian accent, wonderful red hair, an artistic eye, and a wicked sense of humor. Taylor kept an eye on me, and at the end of the production, he produced a brilliant music video of David Bowie’s title song, which Jimmy Murakami directed.

While helping me fact-check my story, Taylor furnished a cavalcade of details. The following are highlights:

TVC was the creative hub of the animation industry in London for nearly four decades. The studio was the ‘Fisher’s Folly’ of our time [an expansive home to great talent in 16th-century London]… It functioned as a significant cultural node within an expanding network of just about anyone in the business of film production at a time that predated the mouse and keyboard—all before closing time on the last years of the ‘golden age of handmade British animation.’

During the making of the film, the rendering technique that followed on from The Snowman brought about the first ‘strike’ in [U.K.] animation employment history by the newly formed rendering crew. Rendering became a recognized skill acquired through experience and the discipline of animating color in much the same way as animating line created the illusion of movement; however, the combination of the two unique skills kept the action in tune with the illustrated narrative of Briggs’ work. TVC inherited the reputation of ‘rendering color’ by way of the late Jill Brooks (1948–2025), who brought her experience of working on the copulating flowers sequence in Pink Floyd: The Wall (1982) to Dianne Jackson’s superbly directed The Snowman.

From the start, When the Wind Blows was John Coates’ personal project. When acquiring the rights to The Snowman, John astutely acquired first option on all of Briggs’ work, which in 1979 had yet to be fully appreciated and [was] technically far from easily adapted. Lee Stork, a maverick producer of commercials and short films, often lunched with John at the Gay Hussar [a Hungarian restaurant in Soho], and he gave John the confidence to single-handedly tackle a feature film that had serious social and political overtones. To John’s credit, he remained politically neutral throughout, claiming the film—faithful to Briggs’ book—didn’t need to be associated with any one organization. I thought that was particularly representative of his true charismatic character, which, although affable on the surface, was made of stern stuff. Even though TVC suffered from the lack of support from the anti-nuke movements and seemingly was in the lee of that network, When the Wind Blows fortunately, but slowly, gained the respect of the establishment that later backed the Peter Rabbit series (2012) and two features, The Wind in the Willows (1995) and The Willows in Winter (1996).

As an aside, When the Wind Blows is dedicated to [seven] children born during the making, one of whom was my eldest son, William. There were many artists I could single out [for praise], but it’s their personalities and talents that make them the mysterious Shakespeares of the golden age whose work will be their mark.

Australia’s The Amazing Digital Circus, Murder Drones, and Knights of Guinevere studio, Glitch Productions, has greenlit a full season of Gameoverse, the animated action-comedy created by Ross O’Donovan (known online as RubberRoss). The announcement follows the release of the show’s pilot in May, which the studio says has attracted more than 31 million views.

The show’s second episode will premiere May 21, 2027.

Set in a digital universe where each planet functions as a separate video game, Gameoverse follows Kit and Team Nimble as they try to prevent those worlds from being destroyed. The catch: when a hero meets a game’s win condition, the planet is obliterated, releasing an energy source called Float. Saving the world means keeping its villain undefeated.

That puts the team in conflict with Syntax, which manipulates heroes into winning games to harvest the resulting energy.

“I’m happy to share with you all that more Gameoverse is coming!” O’Donovan said. “I’m excited for you all to see what me and my extraordinary team have been cooking. Thank you for your continued support!”

Glitch co-founder Luke Lerdwichagul added:

With the greenlight of Gameoverse – we’re incredibly excited to bring Ross’s world to life who’s been crafting the show with more than a decade of meticulous dedication. The characters, worlds and stories he has created are wonderfully distinctive and diverse, making this a fantastic addition to Glitch’s lineup of shows.

We understand that this project is more than just a story for Ross. A deeply personal work that has been years in the making. We’re committed to honoring that vision and bringing it to the screen with the care it deserves.

The pilot’s voice cast includes Erica Lindbeck as Kit, alongside Chris Sabat, Elsie Lovelock, Michael Cusack, Arin Hanson, JSchlatt, and O’Donovan. Video game composers Grant Kirkhope (Banjo-Kazooie) and Jake Kaufman (Shantae) contribute music.

Tokyo International Film Festival’s Animation Lineup Aims To Bring Creators And Audiences Together

By Cartoon Brew Connect | 10/23/2026 9:23 am | Be the First to Comment!

The Tokyo International Film Festival is looking beyond Japan’s domestic animation hits with this year’s Animation Selection, bringing together films and filmmakers from around the world. Alongside acclaimed international titles and premieres of new Japanese works, the program includes discussions about the medium’s present and future.

That’s the goal of Ryota Fujitsu, programming advisor for the festival’s animation section. With Japan already hosting animation festivals in Niigata, Aichi, and Hiroshima, Fujitsu wants Tokyo’s program to broaden audiences’ perceptions of what animation can offer. Although Japan’s animation industry is among the world’s largest, with revenue reaching almost ¥4 trillion ($25.6 billion) in 2024, Fujitsu says Japanese audiences tend to watch domestic animated films and television rather than work from other countries.

By introducing films acclaimed at international events such as Annecy, the festival hopes to encourage Japanese audiences to explore further. This year’s selection includes the Japanese premieres of Iron Boy and DreamWorks’ Forgotten Island, alongside Érica Maradona’s Son of a Bitch, a coming-of-age story told with a limited color palette. Alexandre Poncet’s documentary Walking with Animators explores animators’ creative processes and what their work means to them, a subject with particular resonance amid debates over AI.

A festival screening can help build a film’s profile in Japan. Robot Dreams, which screened at Tokyo in 2023, became a long-running theatrical hit in the country following its 2024 Oscar nomination. Titles including Iron Boy and Amadeo and the Hypothetical New World will be hoping for similar success after this year’s festival.

“We try to be mindful of choosing works that aren’t necessarily what everyone considers the standard of animation,” explains Fujitsu. “We want films that expand what people see as interesting animation, as well. But we don’t want to force something into the festival just to be different, even if it isn’t interesting. So I try to include works that I feel truly have appeal, and that I feel I can explain this appeal in my own words.

“To put it another way, even if it isn’t a commercial hit, festivals offer the chance to see the many unique and challenging films that exist around the world. Foreign feature-length animated films, precisely because the industry in their own countries is small, are often more daring creatively. From a Japanese perspective, it’s a bit like trying foreign food. Trying foreign food you’ve never had before is an interesting experience, so I chose to approach the selection for the festival like that. I hope that by pairing more unconventional Japanese films with international animation we can find a connection.”

The festival is also becoming a launchpad for original Japanese animated features. Despite the industry’s growth, films not based on existing IP have struggled to compete with established franchises at the box office. Three upcoming Japanese features — Ghost – End of Night, Grotesqqque, and Cherry and Virgin — will screen at this year’s event, offering them an opportunity to build an audience ahead of release.

“Japanese animation often gets finished at the very last minute, so it’s previously been quite difficult to screen it as a premiere at the Tokyo International Film Festival,” Fujitsu explains. “However, [the inclusion of films like Grotesqqque and Ghost] reflects a shift in Japanese animation. In recent years, there’s been a trend of developing those kinds of original projects a bit earlier and submitting them to film festivals.”

Beyond screenings, the festival seeks to bring filmmakers together to discuss the industry. As Fujitsu puts it, the aim is to create “opportunities for foreign and Japanese directors to talk” about animation and its ability to connect people across cultures.

One of three symposiums at this year’s festival, The Thrill of Being an Animator, will bring Poncet into conversation with Shingo Natsume and Atsushi Nishigori, whose work is represented in Ghost – End of Night and Grotesqqque, respectively.

The festival will also screen three recent Japanese animated features directed by women, with their directors participating in a symposium about opportunities for women to move into directing. Women currently account for fewer than 5% of feature animation directors both in Japan and internationally.

Participants include Chika Nagaoka, whose 2019 film Detective Conan: The Fist of Blue Sapphire was the franchise’s first feature directed by a woman; Kotono Watanabe, director of 2023’s Gold Kingdom and Water Kingdom; and Ai Yoshimura, who directed last year’s musical adaptation of the landmark shojo manga The Rose of Versailles.

“I’ve wanted to host a symposium with female directors for a long time,” Fujitsu says of the event, titled Women Directors: Diverse Visions. “Over the past 20 years, the number of women in the Japanese animation industry has increased significantly, and now women are working in all sorts of roles all across the industry. Since becoming a director is often the final step in an animator’s career, it’s taken time for the number of female directors to increase even as the number of female animators has grown, and I think as a result we’re in the middle of a transitional period. I wanted to introduce these three female directors as a clear example of the fact that there are female animators out there today, in all sorts of roles.”

Through its mix of original Japanese features, international animation, and discussions among filmmakers, the festival hopes to encourage audiences to seek out unfamiliar work and give creators opportunities to connect.

The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival runs October 26–November 4.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s spotlight series on animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. Films in this series qualified through one of three routes: winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, screening theatrically, or winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is DreamWorks veteran Liron Topaz’s Saba, a hand-drawn film produced by Lirit Rosenzweig Topaz and told in one continuous shot. Its international animation team includes James Baxter, Tim Watts, Matt Williames, Maël Gourmelen, and Sandro Cleuzo. The film qualified for Oscar consideration through a theatrical run and recently won Best Animated Short at the Woodstock Film Festival.

In a world where living things remain grounded while everything else floats upward, a boy and his grandfather share a home secured by ropes. When a violent storm disrupts their life together, the boy begins a journey toward understanding loss. Inspired by Topaz’s relationship with his own grandfather, Saba turns gravity and the instinct to hold on into physical expressions of grief, memory, and the longing for one more moment with someone we love.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Liron Topaz: The story came from something very personal. My grandfather was one of the people who shaped who I am, and losing him left me with this unresolved need for closure. I didn’t want to recreate specific events from our lives, but rather explore what those moments meant to me emotionally. Once I found the concept of a world where gravity became a metaphor for our temporary time here, I felt I finally had the visual language I had been searching for. It gave me a way to talk about grief, memory, and that desire for one more moment without being literal.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

I learned how important it is to trust the emotional core of a film, especially when the process becomes technically complicated. The entire film is one continuous shot, for around 14,000 frames. Animators from different countries in various time zones, and a pipeline that required every section to connect seamlessly to the next. It would have been very easy to let the technical challenge become the focus. I kept coming back to the question of why we were making each choice. The biggest lesson for me was that complexity only matters if, in the end, the audience simply feels something.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

From the very beginning, I wanted the film to feel handmade and intimate, so hand-drawn animation felt like the natural choice. There is something human and imperfect about a drawing that felt right for a story about memory and loss. My biggest inspirations were Michael Dudok de Wit and Mark Baker. They both have a beautiful, simple visual language, and I wanted to capture that charm. I also wanted the camera to feel physical and immersive, as if we were experiencing the journey alongside the characters in real time. That led to telling the entire film without a single cut.

Gravity and the characters’ need to remain tethered are such fundamental rules of the film’s world. How did you decide what those rules would be, and how strictly did you adhere to them while developing the story?

The rule was always very simple: everything living remains grounded, while everything that is not begins floating upward toward the other side. Once we established that, we tried to follow it very strictly because I wanted the world to feel believable, even though it was surreal.

The ropes became a physical expression of our instinct to hold on after loss, to keep the people, memories, and moments we love from drifting away, even when we know we eventually have to let go. Nothing in the film was arbitrary. Every detail carried meaning, either connected to something personal from my life or to the poetic ideas the film explores.
